lesson.title: Flying the Flag: Tracking State with Boolean Variables
lesson.summary: A flag variable is a boolean that starts out False (or True) and flips when something notable happens during a loop, letting the program remember that fact after the loop ends.
lesson.body:
A loop only exists at any given moment inside one iteration. Once the loop moves on to the next item, whatever happened on the previous pass is gone unless something was saved. Sometimes what you need to remember is not a total or a count but a simple yes-or-no fact: did any negative number ever appear, did the password ever get entered correctly, is the list already sorted. A flag variable answers exactly this kind of question. It is a boolean variable, typically initialized before the loop to False, that gets set to True the moment the condition it is watching for becomes true, and then stays True for the rest of the program's life (or at least until it is deliberately reset).

The flag pattern is a direct application of the boolean type combined with the general shape of loop patterns you have already seen with counters. Where a counter accumulates a number, a flag accumulates a single bit of memory: has this happened yet, at any point. The update inside the loop is not an augmented assignment like += 1, because a boolean does not add up, it simply gets overwritten with True (or occasionally back to False) whenever the triggering condition is met.

Here is a flag that checks whether a list contains any negative number:

numbers = [4, 7, 2, 9, 3]
found_negative = False
for n in numbers:
    if n < 0:
        found_negative = True
print(found_negative)

Trace through it. found_negative starts False. Each value, 4, 7, 2, 9, and 3, is checked against n < 0, and none of them are negative, so the if block never runs and found_negative is never touched. After the loop finishes, print(found_negative) outputs False, correctly reporting that no negative number was found.

Notice what the flag buys you that a plain if statement inside the loop cannot: the answer survives past the last line of the loop. Without found_negative, the fact that no number was negative would only be knowable one comparison at a time, disappearing as soon as the loop moved to the next item. The flag variable is what turns a series of individual, temporary observations into a single durable conclusion the rest of the program can act on, for example printing a warning message or choosing a different branch of code based on whether found_negative ended up True or False.

A subtlety worth naming: once a flag flips to True inside a loop, most programs never need to flip it back to False during that same pass, because the question being asked ('did this ever happen') only needs one True to be answered for good. That is different from a counter, which keeps changing throughout the loop, and it is also why flags pair so naturally with the break statement in later patterns: once the flag has been set, there is often no reason to keep checking the remaining items at all.

Flags also show up outside of loops entirely, anywhere a program needs to remember a yes-or-no condition across multiple steps: whether a file successfully opened, whether a user is currently logged in, whether a game is still running. The naming convention matters for readability too. A flag variable is almost always named to read like a question with an implied 'is' or 'has,' such as found_negative, is_valid, or has_submitted, so that later code checking if found_negative reads naturally as a sentence rather than as an obscure abbreviation.
